articles.headline: A BTS star visits an old pyramid in Lima
articles.standfirst: After a big concert, the leader of the band went to see a very old place in Miraflores.
body: BTS, the famous band from South Korea, is in Lima this week. On Wednesday, the band played a big concert at San Marcos Stadium. Thousands of fans came to see them. BTS fans call themselves 'ARMY'.
On Thursday, the band's leader, RM, shared some photos on Instagram. In them, he is visiting Huaca Pucllana, an old pyramid in the Miraflores district of Lima. His real name is Kim Nam-joon.
Huaca Pucllana is very, very old. People from the Lima culture built it between about 200 and 700 AD, before the time of the Incas. They made it from adobe and clay.
In one photo, RM is wearing a colourful chullo. This is a traditional Peruvian hat made of wool. Fans in Peru loved the photos and shared them on social media.
BTS has two more concerts in Lima, on 9 and 10 October. On Thursday, fans could buy some extra tickets online.

glossary.d: a group of people who play music together
a show where people play music for an audience
a very big building with a square base and sides that get smaller at the top
a kind of heavy earth that becomes hard when it is dry
made or done in the same way for a very long time

How did RM share his photos?
Who built Huaca Pucllana?
What is a chullo?
When could fans buy extra tickets?

articles.headline: Police find two stolen Renoir paintings
articles.standfirst: The paintings disappeared from a museum in France last month. Now six people have been arrested.
body: Pierre-Auguste Renoir was a famous French painter. There is a museum about him in Cagnes-sur-Mer, a town in the south of France.

Last month, thieves went into the museum early in the morning. They cut a fence and climbed through a window. They took four paintings, but they left two of them when they ran away. The thieves were very fast: everything took less than three minutes!
The two missing paintings were 'Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano' and 'Young Woman at the Well'. Police all over France looked for them.

On Friday, the town said that the police had found the two paintings and arrested six people. The town's mayor, Bryan Masson, was very happy. He said that the paintings are part of the town's history.

a building where people can look at old or important things, like art

articles.headline: 342 pieces of Peru's history come home
articles.standfirst: Objects that had left the country have been given back to the Ministry of Culture. It is the biggest return of the year so far.
body: Peru has recovered 342 objects that are part of its cultural heritage. On Wednesday, the Foreign Affairs Minister, Carlos Espa, handed the items over to the Culture Minister, Alberto Beingolea, at a ceremony at Torre Tagle Palace in Lima. It was the third ceremony of this kind this year, and the largest return so far.

The objects were found abroad and brought back with the help of Peru's embassies in Germany, Argentina, Belgium, Brazil, the United States and the United Kingdom. Police in several countries, including the FBI in the US, also helped. Some people in other countries returned objects voluntarily.

Among the treasures is a large painting called 'The Transit of St. Joseph', which is important for both history and art. There is also a manuscript called 'Ancient Peruvian Art', a unique work with watercolour pictures that is very valuable for researchers.

Minister Espa said that bringing these objects home means they can be protected, studied and passed on to future generations. He explained that protecting heritage is a priority of Peru's foreign policy, and that the country will work with others to stop the illegal trade in cultural objects.

According to the Culture Minister, this work never stops. His team even checks social media, where people often offer these objects for sale. Soon, the public will be able to see the returned items at a special exhibition at the Ministry of Culture.

glossary.d: the history, buildings, art and traditions that a country has from the past
a formal public event to celebrate or mark something important
a book or document written by hand, not printed
all the people born at about the same time, for example children, parents and grandparents
a public show of objects or art, for example in a museum

articles.headline: A classroom full of elephants
articles.standfirst: University students from four countries are learning how to protect one of Africa's greatest wetlands.
body: Imagine a classroom where elephants play near the water and hippos swim past your boat. For a group of more than 20 university students from Australia, Botswana, the United States and the United Kingdom, this is real. They are taking part in a one-week course in the Okavango Delta, in Botswana.

The delta is a huge wetland of islands, woodlands and flood plains that covers more than two million hectares. It is on the UNESCO World Heritage list. Unusually, the Okavango River does not reach the sea. Its water starts as rain in the highlands of Angola, flows through Namibia and ends in the Kalahari Desert in Botswana, where it floods the land every winter.

The area is home to an amazing variety of wildlife, including more than 440 kinds of birds. Botswana has about 130,000 elephants. The students also learn about African wild dogs, which are endangered. Only about 7,000 of them remain.

But the delta has problems. Mpaphi Casper Bonyongo, who runs the Okavango Research Institute, says the biggest threat is farms upstream, which are growing very fast. The floods have also become smaller over the years, probably because of climate change. Because the river crosses three countries, Angola, Namibia and Botswana have to manage it together.
For Sophie Nguyen, a 20-year-old student from Australia, the course has been unlike anything she has done before. 'It feels magical being here,' she said.

glossary.d: an area of land that is very wet and often covered with water
a hectare is a piece of land of 10,000 square metres
animals and plants that live in nature, not with people
in danger of disappearing from the world for ever
in the direction the water of a river comes from

options: It flows into the sea in Namibia.

options: as rain in the highlands of Angola

options: farms upstream that are growing fast

articles.instructions: For each question, choose the paragraph (A–E). Each paragraph can be chosen once.
articles.headline: A 2,500-year-old ski? Melting ice reveals the secrets of the Alps
articles.standfirst: As Switzerland's glaciers shrink, archaeologists are racing to collect objects that have been frozen for thousands of years.
body: A. The Alps are losing their ice faster than almost anywhere else on Earth. Switzerland alone has lost almost a fifth of its ice in just five years. For climate scientists, these figures are alarming. For archaeologists, however, they have created an unexpected and urgent opportunity: objects that have been locked in the ice for thousands of years are now appearing on the surface.

B. One of these archaeologists is Romain Andenmatten, a 42-year-old who works for the Swiss canton of Valais. On a sunny morning recently, while exploring what remains of the ice at a mountain pass called Col de Barberine, he noticed a grey piece of wood, almost a metre long, lying between rocks at the edge of the ice.

C. It was not the first time the pass had surprised him. Three years earlier, at the same spot, about 2,300 metres above sea level, he had found a similar wooden plank. One end of it became narrower, which suggested that it might have been a ski or a snowshoe. Scientists used carbon dating, a method that measures how much of a certain type of carbon is left in old material, to work out its age. The result: it came from around the fifth century BC, during the Iron Age.

D. Nobody knows exactly what happened to its owner. One possibility is that someone crossing the Alps around 2,500 years ago slipped, lost it in the snow and left it behind. The ice then hid it until now.

E. Ice is an excellent protector of the past, because it stops wood, leather and other materials from rotting. But once these objects are exposed to air and sunlight, they can be damaged quickly. That is why archaeologists are now searching mountain passes before the ice, and the history inside it, disappears for good.

glossary.d: scientists who study the past by finding and examining old objects and buildings
a low place between mountains where people can cross from one side to the other
a long, flat piece of wood
a scientific way of finding out how old something that was once alive is
slowly being destroyed by natural processes, like old food or wet wood

questions.q: Which paragraph explains how scientists found out the age of an object?
Which paragraph describes a discovery made recently at the edge of the ice?
Which paragraph suggests a possible story behind an ancient object?
Which paragraph explains why archaeologists need to work quickly?
Which paragraph presents bad news for one group of experts as good news for another?

articles.headline: Nobel Peace Prize goes to a judge who fought for justice
articles.standfirst: Navi Pillay, a lawyer from South Africa, has been honoured for a lifetime of work defending international law.
body: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, a South African human rights lawyer and judge. The Norwegian Nobel Committee, which announced the decision in Oslo on Friday, said she had won the prize "for her efforts to promote peace and international law".

Ms Pillay was born in Durban, South Africa, at a time when the country was ruled under apartheid, a system that separated people by race. Her family is of Indian Tamil origin. As a young lawyer, she defended Nelson Mandela and other people who opposed apartheid.

Later, her career took her to the international stage. She served as a judge on the tribunal that investigated the 1994 genocide in Rwanda and at the International Criminal Court, and she was also the United Nations' top human rights official. More recently, she led a UN commission that investigated the war in Gaza. Israel's government strongly criticised the decision to give her the prize.

Surprisingly, Ms Pillay did not know she had won when the news was announced. She was attending a conference of human rights lawyers in Nuremberg, Germany, and the chair of the committee, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, joked that if she saw a Norwegian number calling, she should pick up. When the news reached the conference, about 120 people burst into applause.

Ms Pillay dedicated the award to the survivors of international crimes and to those who defend international justice. She said it seemed fitting to hear the news in Nuremberg, the city where trials after the Second World War helped to create the modern system of international justice. This year, 287 candidates were nominated. The prize, worth about 1.2 million US dollars, will be presented on 10 December.

glossary.d: a system in South Africa, until the early 1990s, that kept people of different races apart and treated them unequally
a special court that is set up to judge a particular kind of case
the sound of people clapping their hands to show they are pleased

officially suggested as a possible winner of a prize

options: for writing about the history of South Africa

options: She worked for the Nobel Committee.

options: Ms Pillay had not yet been told that she had won.

questions.q: Why did Nuremberg seem a fitting place to hear the news?
options: It is where Ms Pillay was born.

articles.headline: Power-hungry chips push Taiwan to rethink nuclear energy
articles.standfirst: A decade after turning its back on nuclear power, the island is preparing to restart a reactor, and the debate is far from settled.
body: For a decade, Taiwan steadily phased out nuclear power, filling the gap with natural gas and renewable energy. The last plant to close, Maanshan in the island's south, was shut down in May last year. Now, in a striking reversal, the government is preparing to bring it back. Last month, Taiwan's Nuclear Safety Commission said it had completed its review of plans to restart a reactor there, which, according to Taiwan's Central News Agency, could be generating electricity again as early as 2028.

What has changed? Above all, demand. Taiwan's semiconductor and artificial intelligence industries consume ever larger amounts of electricity, and the government expects demand to rise by about 2.5 per cent a year, driven partly by chips, data centres and AI. Several power cuts have also sharpened concern about energy security. The island imports around 96 per cent of its total energy supply. Last year, liquefied natural gas produced about 47 per cent of its electricity, coal 35 per cent and renewables just over 13 per cent, well short of the 20 per cent target that had been set for 2025.

Relying on imported gas has also proved costly. According to Tsung-Kuang Yeh, a dean of nuclear science at National Tsing Hua University, prices soared after Russia invaded Ukraine and spiked again this year with the conflict between the United States and Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Public opinion appears to be shifting too. After the Fukushima disaster in Japan in 2011, the debate focused on how quickly Taiwan, which lies in an earthquake-prone region, could abandon nuclear energy. Yet in a referendum last year, about 4.3 million people voted to reopen the plant, against 1.5 million who opposed it, although the result was rejected because overall turnout was too low. Another referendum, in November, will ask whether the government should abolish its 'Nuclear-Free Homeland' policy.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics argue that Maanshan is too small to make a real difference given the scale of the AI boom, and that radioactive waste and the risk of accidents remain serious concerns. Environmental campaigners would rather see investment in renewables and energy storage, while admitting that both require major upgrades to the grid. Taiwan's dilemma, in other words, is one that many countries now face: how to power a digital economy without sacrificing either security or safety.

glossary.d: stopped using something gradually, step by step, over a period of time
a change to the opposite of what was happening or planned before
a material used to make the chips inside computers, phones and other electronic devices

articles.headline: A flash from the early universe: the most distant radio burst ever detected
articles.standfirst: A pulse of radio waves that set off when the universe was young could help astronomers measure the matter nobody can see.
body: More than ten billion years ago, long before the Earth or the Sun existed, something in a small, distant galaxy released a sudden flash of energy. That signal has only now been detected, and astronomers believe it is the most distant fast radio burst (FRB) ever recorded, more than twice as far away as the previous record holder.

FRBs are intense pulses of radio waves that last mere milliseconds, yet can release as much energy in that instant as the Sun does in months or even years. Since the first one was spotted in 2007, more than 10,000 have been detected. Some repeat constantly, some repeat for a while and then fall silent, and others appear once and are never seen again. Their cause remains a mystery. One leading theory links them to magnetars, a type of neutron star with an extremely powerful magnetic field, although some people have even speculated that they could be alien in origin.

The new burst, catalogued as FRB 20240304B and described in the journal Science, was picked up by the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa. Researchers then used NASA's James Webb Space Telescope to identify the galaxy it came from. The burst began its journey when the universe was only about three billion years old, which means it has crossed roughly 80 per cent of cosmic history. Its home, according to Dr Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney, one of the lead researchers, is a young, very small galaxy forming stars at great speed and containing few metals, a detail that any explanation of FRBs will now have to account for.

Remarkably, scientists do not need to know what causes FRBs in order to make use of them. As the waves travel, they are affected by the particles they pass through, so they act as a kind of cosmic measuring tape for matter that ordinary telescopes cannot see. Prof Matthew Bailes of Swinburne University, one of the astronomers who first discovered FRBs, described them as "a very fundamental way of counting how many atoms there are in the universe". Another Swinburne astrophysicist, Dr Sara Webb, who was not involved in the study, said the discovery suggests that FRBs might have been very common in the early universe.

glossary.d: a millisecond is one thousandth of a second
dead stars that are extremely dense and have an extraordinarily strong magnetic field
officially recorded in a list with a name or number
relating to the whole universe
a scientist who studies the physical nature of stars, planets and the universe

questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose in the first paragraph?
options: to explain how radio telescopes work
to criticise the previous distance record
to emphasise how old and distant the signal is
to compare the Earth with the Sun

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about the cause of FRBs?
options: It has finally been identified as magnetars.
It is still unknown, although there are several theories.
It has been shown to be alien.
It depends on how many FRBs repeat.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, what does "it" in "the galaxy it came from" refer to?
Why is the type of galaxy where the burst began significant?
options: It proves that FRBs come from our own galaxy.
It shows that FRBs only happen in large, old galaxies.
It means that the burst will certainly repeat.
Any theory of FRBs must explain how they can occur in young galaxies with few metals.

questions.q: According to the article, what can FRBs be used for?
options: predicting where new stars will form
measuring matter that ordinary telescopes cannot detect
finding planets similar to the Earth
